newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italian markets brush off Prodi scare.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italian markets brush off Prodi scare.

text.p: Italian financial markets brushed aside political jitters about Prime Minister Romano Prodi's legal problems on Tuesday, looking instead to interest rate prospects after the lira's return to Europe's currency grid.

The lira, getting used to its new status in the exchange rate mechanism, cut a stable but unobtrusive figure on foreign exchange markets and held near its 990 per mark central parity on its second day in the grid after a four year absence.
"If the rest of the currency market can remain stable the lira can do better -- unless we have any major political scandals," said one foreign exchange dealer at an Italian bank.
News on Monday that an Italian magistrate wanted Prodi sent to trial for alleged abuse of office when he was chairman of state industrial holding IRI in 1993 bruised markets at the time.
But bond traders said investors were more sanguine by Tuesday and positive sentiment was stealing back.

"There was a bad reaction on Prodi initially but the market is largely ignoring it now. The investigation has been going on for some time and Prodi himself seems pretty relaxed about it," a futures broker at an Italian bank in London said.

Prodi, who was already questioned in the inquiry in March, has said he is confident Italy's judicial system will clear him. His office said on Tuesday he not yet been advised officially that an indictment had been sought.

By 1315 GMT the lira was quoted at 991.50 per mark after touching 990.75 earlier, while the December Btp future on LIFFE was 40 basis points higher on the day, slightly below a record high set after the lira's ERM return on Monday.

Traders cited healthy buying interest from U.S., Japanese and domestic Italian investors, and said the bond market's fall on Monday after the Prodi news ultimately served as a chance for people to pick up Italian assets at cheap rates.
On the stock market, which opened late due to a technical hitch, the blue-chip Mib30 index made up for the delay by climbing nearly half a percentage point to 15,745.
Giuseppe Bonini, head of the dealing room at Milan brokers Intersim, said the initial buoyant effect of the lira's return to the ERM was now fading away.
"Instead the market is looking ahead to a stable lira, a steady fall in the inflation rate and an interest rate cut before the end of the year," Bonini said.

Economists polled by Reuters earlier this week showed most expect the Bank of Italy to lop half a percentage point off its key discount rate, currently at 7.5 percent, at least by the year end and more likely by mid-December.

Analysts say the central bank wants to see how the lira takes to its new ERM environment before it lowers interest rates, given that the currency went back into the grid at a stronger rate than the Italian government originally wanted.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi also directed attention to the long term, sobering implications of being back in the ERM, stressing Italy could not afford to slacken efforts to meet economic criteria for European monetary union.
"We need to be very aware that re-entry in the ERM is something very different from entry into the single European currency," Ciampi told the budget committee of Italy's Senate or upper house.
